title: Debugging Networking Inside Kubernetes
intro: Inside a cluster, the same layered approach applies — DNS, then port, then application — but you have to run the checks from INSIDE a pod, because that's where the traffic actually originates.

steps.prompt: From inside the 'web' pod, check whether the 'orders' service name resolves.
steps.explanation: CoreDNS (10.96.0.10) resolved 'orders' to its ClusterIP via the pod's search domains.
steps.why: Running nslookup from your laptop tests the wrong resolver entirely. Cluster DNS only works from inside the cluster, which is why every in-cluster network check starts with kubectl exec.

steps.prompt: DNS works. Now test the actual HTTP endpoint from inside the pod.
steps.fake_output: curl: (7) Failed to connect to orders port 8080: Connection refused
steps.explanation: Refused — the Service exists, but nothing is answering behind it on that port.
steps.why: Same refused-vs-timeout logic as anywhere else: refused points at the backends (no ready pods, or the wrong targetPort), a timeout would point at a NetworkPolicy dropping traffic.

steps.prompt: Check whether the service actually has any backend pods behind it.
steps.explanation: Two backends exist — listening on port 3000, not 8080.
steps.why: The Service's targetPort (3000) routes correctly, but the client called port 8080, which the Service doesn't expose. Comparing the port you call against 'kubectl get svc orders' output resolves it.

steps.prompt: Check for NetworkPolicies in the namespace that could restrict traffic.
steps.explanation: A policy selects the orders pods — anything not explicitly allowed by it is dropped.
steps.why: Even after fixing the port, if 'web' isn't matched by allow-frontend's ingress rules, requests will time out instead of being refused. Rule out policies explicitly rather than assuming traffic is allowed.

steps.prompt: Bypass all in-cluster routing and reach the orders service from your laptop on local port 9090.
steps.explanation: localhost:9090 now tunnels straight to an orders pod through the Kubernetes API.
steps.why: port-forward skips Ingress, load balancers, and NetworkPolicies. If the app works through port-forward but not through the normal path, you've proven the app is fine and the problem is in the routing layers you just bypassed.
